meta.title: AI safety concern directory — source index

verified.true: The URL or address was fetched during research and the contact route was seen on the page itself.
verified.false: The route is cited by a secondary source but the page could not be read. Treat as a lead to confirm, not an address to rely on.
verified.null: Not independently checked. Applies to homepage and framework links, which were recorded as listed rather than confirmed.

entity_public_input.open: Publishes a route a member of the public can use without affiliation or credentials.
entity_public_input.limited: Has a route, but it is restricted by constituency, membership, account status, programme invitation, or language.
entity_public_input.none: Publishes no public contact route for this purpose. Recorded deliberately — absence is a finding.

value_kind.other: Postal address, phone number or free text

dataset.register: AI Safety Concern Register — 229 institutions and their contact routes.
dataset.seats: Where to Take an AI Concern — committees and bodies with AI jurisdiction.
dataset.organisations: Where to Take an AI Concern — campaigns, civil society, professional and industry bodies.

caveats: Compiled 22 September 2026. Contact routes move; named seat-holders move faster.
129 of the register's 589 routes are unverified and are marked as such.
The UK's DSIT was abolished in July 2026 and the Commons committee reverted to its former name; some register entries written against the older structure are partly stale.
The International Network of AI Safety Institutes was renamed in December 2025, dropping 'safety' from its title.
Non-US, non-EU committee entries rely on bodies reconstituted annually; Indian and Japanese chairs in particular should be re-confirmed.
No email address or URL in this dataset was generated. Where a route could not be found, the record says so rather than guessing.

sources.label: Model safety issues and jailbreaks
sources.scope: Safety issues, jailbreaks, harmful model behaviour. Named on both the Responsible Disclosure Policy and the Usage Policy.
sources.note: The single most useful address for a member of the public with a model-behaviour concern. Anthropic asks for 'sufficient details for us to replicate the issue'.

sources.label: Questions about the disclosure policy
sources.scope: Questions about the Responsible Disclosure Policy itself, not for submitting reports.
sources.note: Policy questions only; actual reports go to HackerOne or usersafety@.

sources.label: Responsible Disclosure Policy
sources.scope: Infrastructure vulnerabilities AND model safety. States: 'We welcome reports concerning safety issues, "jailbreaks," and similar concerns so that we can enhance the safety and harmlessness of our models.'
sources.note: Unusual among labs in explicitly putting model safety inside the disclosure policy rather than excluding it.

sources.label: HackerOne submission form
sources.scope: Vulnerability submissions under the Responsible Disclosure Policy.
sources.note: Embedded form, no HackerOne account gatekeeping described on the policy page.

sources.label: Model Safety Bug Bounty Program (application)
sources.scope: Universal jailbreaks that defeat Constitutional Classifiers, especially CBRN. Up to $35,000 per novel universal jailbreak.
sources.note: Application-only and invite-based via HackerOne; participation requires an NDA. Program details: https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12119250-model-safety-bug-bounty-program

sources.label: Usage Policy / Trust & Safety appeals
sources.scope: Appealing enforcement decisions against your own account.
sources.note: Not a safety-reporting channel; for account holders only.

sources.label: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, Version 3.4 (effective 8 July 2026)
Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure Policy
sources.scope: States: 'We invite you to report vulnerabilities, bugs, safety and abuse issues, or security flaws you discover in our systems.'
sources.note: Broad invitation on its face, but the operative programs are on Bugcrowd and split security from safety.

sources.label: OpenAI Bug Bounty (Bugcrowd)
sources.scope: Infrastructure/product security. $200 to $20,000.
sources.note: URL cited on OpenAI's own policy page; Bugcrowd page is JS-rendered and could not be read directly.

sources.label: OpenAI Safety Bug Bounty (Bugcrowd)
sources.scope: Model safety / CBRN jailbreaks. Separate engagement from the main bounty.
sources.note: Linked from OpenAI's coordinated disclosure policy. AI Frontiers reports all prompts, completions, findings and communications under it are NDA-covered — you cannot publish what you find.

sources.label: Report Content
sources.scope: Publicly open form for policy violations and illegal content: violence and self-harm, sexual exploitation, child exploitation, bullying, fraud, privacy, IP.
sources.note: The only genuinely open, no-account-needed public channel. It is a content/abuse route, not an alignment route.

sources.label: Researcher Access Program
sources.scope: Open and active. Up to $1,000 of API credits for 'researchers using our products to study areas related to the responsible deployment of AI and mitigating associated risks'. Reviewed quarterly.
sources.note: Explicitly welcomes 'early stage researchers' and those with 'limited financial and institutional resources'. Low-friction way in.

sources.label: Red Teaming Network
sources.scope: External domain experts stress-testing models.
sources.note: CLOSED. Page states 'Applications are now closed' (deadline was 1 December 2023); says it may reopen. Do not count on it.

sources.label: Model behavior feedback form
sources.scope: DEPRECATED. Page now reads: 'We've deprecated this web form in favor of other channels.'
sources.note: Redirects you to in-product thumbs-down, the API dashboard, or support. A named safety channel that was closed.

sources.label: Model Spec feedback form
sources.scope: CLOSED. 'This feedback form is now closed.'
sources.note: The public-comment process on the Model Spec no longer exists; updates are now published to a GitHub page instead.

sources.label: Preparedness Framework v2.0 (15 April 2025); Frontier Governance Framework (May 2026); Model Spec (updated continuously)
Google AI Vulnerability Reward Program
sources.scope: Security vulnerabilities in AI products. Jailbreaks and in-session harmful content generation are EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE.
sources.note: Page returns HTTP 200 but is fully JS-rendered and could not be read as text. Scope confirmed by a researcher who published Google's verbatim rejection (below).

sources.label: Gemini content reporting (legal troubleshooter)

sources.note: Cited from Gemini's policy guidelines page. A legal/removal route, not a safety-research route.

sources.label: In-product thumbs-down on Gemini output
sources.scope: The only routine route for flagging a bad model response.

sources.label: Advanced AI Scaling Framework, Version 2 (7 April 2026)
MSRC Researcher Portal
sources.scope: Security vulnerability submissions including AI systems, graded against the AI bug bar.
sources.note: Also reachable as aka.ms/secure-at per the Copilot bounty page.

sources.label: Microsoft Copilot AI Bounty
sources.scope: $250-$30,000. Security vulnerabilities in Copilot surfaces. Explicitly EXCLUDES 'AI prompt injection attacks that do not have a security impact on users other than the attacker', 'model hallucination where the model pretends to run arbitrary code', and 'attacks that aim to leak (part of) the system/meta prompt'. Content issues must be reported separately as 'AI derived harm'.
sources.note: One of the clearest published statements anywhere that jailbreak-style findings are not a bounty item.

sources.label: AI/ML Vulnerability Severity Classification (AI bug bar)
sources.scope: Splits AI issues into security vulnerabilities (CVSS-rated: inference manipulation, membership inference, model theft) and Responsible AI issues (hate speech, misinformation, sexual content, self-harm) classified only 'In Scope' or 'Out of Scope for investigation, without severity ratings'.
sources.note: Notably says Microsoft 'actively welcome[s] submissions related to safety and societal harm' — a rare explicit invitation. CSEAM must go to Report a Concern instead.

sources.label: Report a Concern (Digital Safety)
sources.scope: Harmful content across Microsoft services, including AI-generated.
sources.note: The consumer-facing route MSRC redirects content reports to.

sources.label: Enterprise AI Services abuse report
sources.scope: Reporting abusive, illegal or infringing use of a Microsoft AI Service.
sources.note: Published in the Code of Conduct for Microsoft AI Services.

sources.label: Bounty terms and conditions
sources.scope: Section 8 provides a limited exemption from reverse-engineering restrictions where 'The actions were performed during good-faith security research, which was — or was intended to be — responsibly reported to Apple'.
sources.note: This is the safe-harbour language, and it is narrow: it covers reverse engineering, not a general no-legal-action promise, and applies only within the program terms.

Submission page
sources.scope: A flaw, vulnerability or incident in any AI system. This is the first live implementation of the standardised AI flaw report concept — it covers model-behaviour flaws, biases and incidents, not only security bugs.
sources.note: Guided web form at ai-reports.org ('Report Now'), takes roughly 10 minutes and generates a standardised, machine-readable flaw report. You then choose where to route it: the site lists Anthropic, Hugging Face, Cohere, the UK AI Safety/Security Institute, CERT/CC, ECDA and DAVID as recipients. You can also take the generated report and submit it yourself anywhere, or go direct to CERT/CC's VINCE.

sources.label: Submission page
sources.scope: N/A — it is the proposal document that defines the emerging norm. Read it to understand the vocabulary that labs and coordinators are converging on.
sources.note: Three proposals: (1) standardised flaw reports and published rules of engagement, so researchers know what they may test and how to report; (2) broadly-scoped disclosure programs with legal safe harbours modelled on bug bounties; (3) coordinated distribution infrastructure, because jailbreaks and flaws transfer across providers. Its practical successor is FLARE-AI, which implements the standardised report and the distribution layer.

sources.entity: 'In-House Evaluation Is Not Enough' — third-party AI flaw disclosure framework
sources.label: Homepage
Submission page
sources.scope: Two distinct lanes, and the distinction is the whole point. Security lane (via HackerOne): misconfigurations, CSRF, privilege escalation, SQL injection, XSS, directory traversal on internet-facing systems. Model-safety lane (via email): the policy states explicitly 'We welcome reports concerning safety issues, "jailbreaks," and similar concerns so that we can enhance the safety and harmlessness of our models' — these go to usersafety@anthropic.com.
sources.note: Security bugs: submit through Anthropic's HackerOne program with vulnerability type, technical detail, reproduction steps, URLs, PoC and impact. Model behaviour and jailbreaks: email usersafety@anthropic.com. This is the cleanest published example of the procedural split — a model-behaviour finding sent to a security intake will be closed as out of scope, and a security bug emailed to a safety address loses bounty eligibility.

sources.label: Submission page
sources.scope: Universal jailbreaks that defeat Anthropic's Constitutional Classifiers — generalised techniques that work across many prompts, tested against a supplied set of harmful questions concerning CBRN/biological threat information. Narrow, context-specific exploits do not qualify.
sources.note: Complete a Google Form application and create a HackerOne account first. If accepted you receive a HackerOne invitation and must create a Claude Console account using your @wearehackerone.com alias. An NDA is mandatory. Applications reviewed on a rolling basis.

sources.note: Submit via bughunters.google.com under the AI VRP rules. Content and alignment issues go through the thumbs-down / report flows inside Gemini, Search and Workspace.

sources.scope: Serious incidents as defined in Article 3(49), reported by the provider. Deadlines: immediately after establishing a causal link and in any case not later than 15 days after awareness; 2 days for widespread infringement or certain serious incidents; and for a death, immediately after establishing or suspecting a causal relationship and within 10 days maximum. Incomplete initial reports are permitted, followed by a complete report.
sources.note: Indirect only, and this is the practically important point: a member of the public cannot trigger Article 73 directly, but can (a) notify the provider, which starts the provider's own awareness clock and creates evidence of when they knew, and (b) file an Article 85 complaint with the market surveillance authority alleging a serious incident went unreported — failure to report is itself an infringement the authority can act on.

In practice this means internal channels first, then the competent national authority, with external/public disclosure protected in defined circumstances. The AI Office's whistleblower tool is the EU-level external channel.

sources.entity: GDPR Article 77 — complaint to a data protection supervisory authority
sources.label: Submission page
sources.scope: Complaints from any data subject who considers that processing of their personal data infringes the GDPR. You may complain to the authority in your Member State of habitual residence, your place of work, or the place of the alleged infringement.
sources.note: File with the chosen supervisory authority, usually via their online form. Frame the concern in data protection terms — lawful basis, accuracy, transparency, Article 22 automated decision-making — because a concern framed as 'this AI is unsafe' will be rejected as out of scope, while the same facts framed as a data protection issue may be entertained.

sources.label: Homepage
Submission page
sources.scope: Complaints about how an organisation has handled your personal information. General customer service complaints only if combined with a data protection concern.
sources.note: Raise it with the organisation first and give them a chance to put things right, then complain via ico.org.uk/make-a-complaint. Expect the ICO to ask what the organisation said.

sources.entity: Ofcom — individual complaint about an online service
sources.label: Submission page
sources.scope: Complaints about phone, broadband and postal services; TV, radio and on-demand programmes; wireless interference; something you have seen on an online service, website or app; and premium rate services.
sources.note: Contact the service provider first, then report via Ofcom's online complaints portal at ofcom.org.uk/make-a-complaint.

sources.entity: Ofcom — individual complaint about an online service
sources.label: Homepage
Submission page
sources.scope: Complaints from eligible entities about a feature or conduct of one or more regulated services presenting a material risk of significant harm, of significant adverse impact on freedom of expression, or other significant adverse impacts. For a single-service complaint you must additionally explain its particular importance or the scale of user impact.
sources.note: Written submission to Ofcom with organisational contact details, description of the feature or conduct, identification of the services/providers, and evidence of material risk. Supporting evidence must be current, objective and verifiable. An unaffiliated individual's realistic route is to supply evidence to an eligible organisation rather than to file directly.

sources.label: Submission page
sources.scope: Reports of fraud, scams and bad business practices — which covers AI-related deception: false capability claims, deceptive AI marketing, undisclosed AI use, AI-enabled impersonation. The FTC has brought AI-deception cases under its Section 5 unfair-or-deceptive-practices authority.
sources.note: Online at reportfraud.ftc.gov. Note: at the time of this research the site was returning a government shutdown notice and was unable to offer the reporting service, directing users to consumer.ftc.gov instead — verify availability before relying on it. An alternative framing for AI-safety-adjacent harms is a complaint to a State Attorney General.

sources.jurisdiction: California (reaches most major AI developers, which are California-domiciled)
sources.label: Submission page
sources.scope: Complaints about businesses, including AI companies. The AG investigates where complaints suggest patterns of consumer harm or systematic violations of consumer protection law.
sources.note: Online web form at oag.ca.gov, or download, print and mail the form. Forms available in English, Spanish, Chinese and Vietnamese. Provide your contact details, the business's details, the product/service, transaction dates, names of representatives, your desired resolution, and evidence of prior contact attempts with the business.

sources.jurisdiction: California (reaches most major AI developers, which are California-domiciled)
sources.label: Homepage
Submission page
sources.scope: Evidence drawn from research, professional expertise or personal experience. You explicitly do not need to be a formal expert or have any institutional affiliation. Address the questions in the call for evidence; you need not answer all of them.
sources.note: Find an inquiry currently accepting evidence via the committees portal filter (committees.parliament.uk/inquiries/ with 'Currently accepting evidence'), then submit through that inquiry's online portal. At the time of this research 27 inquiries were accepting evidence and none was specifically AI-focused — but AI-relevant evidence is regularly submitted to inquiries on employment, financial services, human rights and public services, and recent AI inquiries (Business and Trade Committee on AI and the future workforce; Treasury Committee on AI in financial services; JCHR on human rights and AI regulation) show the pattern.

sources.entity: NIST / CAISI requests for information on AI
sources.label: Submission page
sources.scope: Technical input from developers, deployers and security researchers on AI security and standards questions. Recent dockets have covered unique security threats to AI agents, security practices and technical controls, assessment methods for identifying and managing AI vulnerabilities, deployment constraints and monitoring, and research and policy priorities.
sources.note: Via regulations.gov using the docket number in the Federal Register notice. Answer the numbered questions directly and in order — this is the single most effective structural choice, because NIST staff synthesise responses question by question.

sources.note: Draft the petition, secure 5 supporters, submit for standards review, and if approved it is published and open for signatures for 6 months.

sources.entity: California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act) — whistleblower protections and public incident reporting
sources.label: Submission page
sources.scope: Two distinct things. (1) Whistleblower protection: employees and contractors of frontier developers are protected against retaliation for reporting activity connected to catastrophic risks — defined around foreseeable risks of a frontier model causing death or serious injury to 50+ people, enabling weapons creation, engaging in criminal conduct without meaningful human intervention, or evading developer control. Employers must give notice of these rights and maintain anonymous internal reporting channels. (2) Developer reporting: frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to OES within 15 days of discovery, or 24 hours where there is imminent danger of death or serious injury.
sources.note: Employees: use the employer's mandated anonymous internal channel, and take legal advice before external disclosure. Critically for this playbook: SB 53 requires OES to establish a mechanism for the public to report critical safety incidents — meaning a member of the public, not just an insider, has a statutory route to a state emergency agency. Verify the current status and URL of that OES mechanism directly with OES before relying on it; implementation detail was not published in the sources reviewed.

sources.entity: AI Whistleblower Protection Act (S.1792) — federal, not law
sources.label: Homepage
Submission page
sources.scope: Concerns from tech and AI workers, at any level of completeness — explicitly including partial information, 'one line of code that is a red flag', or a general unease. Designed as a 'lower stakes way' to report without becoming a formal whistleblower.
sources.note: Deposit information into the secure escrow. The model is the key innovation: multiple people can contribute pieces of a puzzle, and Psst determines whether actionable evidence exists across depositors before anyone has to expose themselves individually. You then receive guidance on appropriate disclosure channels.

sources.label: Submission page

sources.note: Secure contact at thesignalsnetwork.org/contact/. sources.entity: The Signals Network — Tech Accountability Project
sources.label: Homepage
Submission page
sources.scope: People who have discovered illegality, gross mismanagement or waste of funds, or threats to health and safety in their employment. Focus is on widespread, systemic issues affecting the public interest.
sources.note: Complete the intake form at intake.whistleblower.org. Reviewed by staff, with a response typically within about a month. Important: contacting them does not create legal representation and does not toll any statute of limitations — you bear responsibility for your own filing deadlines, which range from 30 days to three years depending on claim type, and GAP will not alert you to them during the application process.

sources.jurisdiction: United States; covers publicly traded companies and securities-law violations
sources.label: Submission page
sources.scope: Original information about potential violations of the federal securities laws. For AI: material misrepresentation of model capability, safety practices or risk to investors — 'AI-washing' cases have been brought. Reaches Google, Microsoft, Meta and Nvidia; reaches private labs only where securities law otherwise bites.
sources.note: Submit through the SEC's Tips, Complaints and Referrals portal (recommended — gives immediate confirmation and a submission number), or mail/fax Form TCR to SEC Office of the Whistleblower, c/o ENF-CPU, 1604 Springhill Road, Suite 110, Vienna, VA 22182, fax +1 703-813-9322. You must answer 'yes' to filing under the whistleblower program and complete the whistleblower declaration to get award eligibility and enhanced confidentiality.

sources.entity: UK Public Interest Disclosure Act — protected disclosure to a prescribed person

sources.entity: 'To Err is AI' — evidence on what makes an LLM flaw report land
sources.label: Submission page
sources.scope: N/A — empirical evidence on flaw reporting practice.
sources.note: Findings from an open-ended bug bounty in August 2024 in which 495 hackers produced evaluations against the OLMo open language model, with cash awards for demonstrated flaws. Practical lesson for a submitter: successful reports did not merely exhibit bad output — they connected the identified issue to a concrete deployment hazard and to a clear need for public disclosure clarifying the intent, capacities and hazards of the deployment. The paper also sets out best practices for safety reporting processes, their artifacts, and safety program staffing.

sources.entity: 'The perils of AI safety's insularity' — why outside contributions get ignored
sources.label: Submission page
sources.scope: N/A
sources.note: N/A — read as diagnosis. Its claims: AI safety has built a parallel research universe outside academia that trades external scrutiny for speed; the network is geographically and financially concentrated (Berkeley/San Francisco, EA-aligned funders); researchers do not meaningfully engage with mainstream ML venues and consequently reinvent existing methods; funding shapes research direction more than consensus does; and there is a reported lower publication bar for optimistic than for critical claims about AI. It cites work arguing 'scheming' research risks repeating failures ape-language researchers made 50 years ago, and Dan Hendrycks calling mechanistic interpretability misguided.

sources.entity: Future Caucus National Task Force on State AI Policy
sources.label: Public submission route

sources.entity: All-Party Parliamentary Group on Artificial Intelligence (APPG AI)
sources.label: Public submission route
sources.scope: Cross-party, cross-House informal group. Its registered purpose: 'The APPG explores the social, economic and societal impact and implications of artificial intelligence.' It has no formal powers but it convenes ministers, officials and MPs, runs evidence sessions and publishes reports — and unlike a select committee it is genuinely open to unsolicited outside contact.
sources.note: VERIFIED 2026-09-22 from the official Register of All-Party Parliamentary Groups as at 29 June 2026. Dr Gardner also sits on the Commons Science and Technology Committee, which makes her the highest-leverage single UK backbench contact on AI.

sources.entity: European Parliament — Committee on the Internal Market and Consumer Protection (IMCO)
sources.label: Public submission route
sources.scope: Co-lead committee on the AI Act and its successors. IMCO owns the AI Act as a product-safety and internal-market instrument: placing AI systems on the market, conformity assessment, high-risk classification, obligations on providers and deployers, and consumer protection. It was joint-lead with LIBE on the Digital Omnibus on AI and is lead on the Cloud and AI Development Act.

sources.entity: e-Gov Public Comment (Administrative Procedure Act public comment procedure)
sources.label: Public submission route
sources.scope: The single mandatory consultation channel for all Japanese ministries when making 命令等 (cabinet orders, ministerial ordinances, notices/告示, administrative guidance). Every AI-related ordinance, notice and Basic Plan draft from the Cabinet Office, METI, MIC and the Digital Agency passes through here. Statutory basis: Administrative Procedure Act (行政手続法), Chapter 6. Policy oversight sits with MIC's A
sources.note: System description, the 30-day statutory floor, the no-account/conditional-fields submission mechanics and the substance-over-volume rule are all VERIFIED from the official e-Gov pages public-comment.e-gov.go.jp/contents/about-public-comment and /contents/help/guide/submission.html. The absence of English support is a verified negative — the official pages carry no language options and no guidance for foreign submitters. The e-Gov top page is JavaScript-rendered and will not load for simple fetchers; the /contents/ subpages do.
sources.language: Japanese only. There is no English interface, no English guidance, and comments are expected in Japanese. Nothing formally bars a non-Japanese speaker or a foreign national from submitting — there is no nationality check — but in practice a submission that officials cannot read will not be processed meaningfully.

sources.jurisdiction: UK, US, Canada, Germany. UK not-for-profit company limited by guarantee; US 501(c)(4).
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Governments should pass binding law prohibiting the development of superintelligent AI, and coordinate internationally to enforce that prohibition.
sources.note: Its own action page says '205+ lawmakers support our campaign'; its homepage breaks that down as 160+ UK and 35+ Canadian lawmakers, plus 400+ lawmakers briefed across four countries. 'Support' means signing a campaign statement, not voting for a bill — no such bill has passed. The ask is a prohibition, not regulation; joining means endorsing a ban. Small donors are effectively not wanted.

sources.jurisdiction: International. Legally Stichting PauseAI (KvK 92951031), Netherlands. Local communities in many countries.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Stop the development of the most powerful general AI systems, internationally, until we know how to make them safe.
sources.note: The ask is a halt to frontier development, not tighter rules. Protest-based but explicitly lawful — distinct from StopAI. Chapters vary a lot in activity; check your local one is alive before committing.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: The United States should lead an international treaty to pause frontier AI development, and should pass domestic bills including a 'kill switch' and an AI Risk Evaluation Act.
sources.note: Legally and financially separate from PauseAI Global (Dutch foundation) and PauseAI UK — a US 501(c)(3) with its own EIN and board. Shares the movement's name and broad ask but sets its own US legislative priorities. The ask is a development pause, which most US lawmakers do not currently support; expect to be advocating a minority position.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: The UK should act to avert risks from superhuman AI, including binding frontier AI legislation.
sources.note: A distinct UK operation with its own staff, site, jobs and donation route — not simply a page of PauseAI Global. Chapter activity is uneven; the newer chapters are very new.

sources.jurisdiction: Primarily San Francisco Bay Area; one protest documented in Kinshasa, DRC.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: A permanent, enforceable global ban on all further development of frontier AI, plus citizen oversight bodies empowered to regulate or dismantle dangerous technologies.
sources.note: This is a civil-disobedience group and you should join only knowing that. Members have blockaded OpenAI's doors and been prosecuted: member Wynd Kaufmyn faced four misdemeanour charges (case CRI-25404422, San Francisco Superior Court), was denied the necessity defence, and the site states she was due to surrender to serve a sentence on 14 Aug 2026. It also subpoenaed Sam Altman (quashed). Its platform is broader than AI risk — it includes rejecting transhumanism and AI personhood, calls for a smaller economy, and bans on AI weapons. Not all actions are legal; attending a protest can carry arrest risk.

sources.entity: Encode (formerly Encode Justice; also Encode AI)
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Pass enforceable AI laws — transparency, safety frameworks, incident reporting, third-party audits and whistleblower protection for frontier AI companies — while keeping AI's benefits.
sources.note: encodejustice.org now redirects to encodeai.org — the youth-chapter branding of Encode Justice has largely been folded into a professional policy shop. Its current site advertises no chapters, no volunteer programme and no membership, so a newcomer's realistic route is donating or being hired, not joining. Its ask is regulation and transparency, explicitly 'pro-human pro-AI' — not a pause or ban.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: AI companies should keep the safety and transparency commitments they have publicly made, and be held accountable when they quietly walk them back.
sources.note: Adversarial toward specific named companies. If you work at an AI lab, sending a tip may breach your employment agreement — take legal advice first; the organisation is small and cannot indemnify you.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: US federal government should build the capacity to see and respond to frontier AI risk — monitoring, standards and emergency powers.
sources.note: FLAG: mostly closed. Do not plan effort around it. Revival contact given on its site is jason@aipolicy.us. This is also a useful data point about the funding asymmetry in this field.

sources.entity: Center for AI Safety Action Fund (CAIS AF)
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: US policy should maintain American leadership in AI while protecting against AI-related national security threats — chip manufacturing leadership, compute security, preventing malicious use, and global cooperation on safe AI.
sources.note: Its framing is national-security and US competitiveness, not a pause or ban — noticeably more hawkish in framing than PauseAI or ControlAI, and it sits comfortably with 'US leadership in AI'. If your goal is slowing AI, check the framing matches your intent. There is essentially no public participation route.

sources.jurisdiction: United States and European Union (Brussels lobbying presence).
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: A moratorium on developing artificial superintelligence for at least 15 years, plus licensing, auditing and enforceable safety standards before scaling — and a participatory global process rather than decisions made by a handful of CEOs.
sources.note: FLI does not have a separately branded advocacy arm — its policy and lobbying work runs through the Institute itself plus EU-registered activity. Its ask is a time-limited moratorium on superintelligence, which is weaker than ControlAI's or StopAI's permanent ban and stronger than Encode's transparency agenda. It is also a funder of other groups on this list, so 'independent' endorsements between these organisations are not always independent.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Raise public awareness of existential risks — above all unaligned AI — because public understanding is the precondition for policy that reduces them.
sources.note: Awareness-raising rather than a campaign you can join. Its donate and get-involved pages could not be retrieved, so treat any volunteering or giving route as UNVERIFIED and email first. Its remit is broader than AI.

sources.entity: CAES — Collective Action for Existential Safety (Center for Existential Safety)
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Individuals, organisations and nations should each take concrete personal action on existential risk — from AI, nuclear weapons and engineered pandemics — starting today.
sources.note: The pledge is demanding: signers commit to 'take at least one action every workday to reduce existential risks until an international body of recognized experts has declared humanity's risk of extinction is under 0.1% per year'. Read that before signing. The site is a directory that points to other organisations — useful as a front door, but joining CAES is not the same as joining a campaign with staff and legislative access.

sources.jurisdiction: United States primarily (the contact tool finds US representatives); global readership.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: A globally coordinated and collectively enforced moratorium on the development of artificial superintelligence, because on current methods the most likely outcome is human extinction.
sources.note: MIRI's stated position is that building superintelligence with current techniques most likely kills everyone. That is the strongest claim on this list; endorsing it publicly has social and professional costs in some workplaces. The DC march is conditional and may never happen.

sources.jurisdiction: France (Paris) and EU-level; registered French nonprofit, reg. no. 919 185 199 00016.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: AI companies should be held to real risk-management standards, and governance should be built on rigorous, auditable frameworks rather than voluntary promises.
sources.note: A research and standards body, not a campaign — there is no membership or activist route. Its ratings are useful ammunition for other people's campaigns.

sources.jurisdiction: Asia, with emphasis on Southeast Asia and middle powers.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Asian institutions — especially Southeast Asian and middle-power states — should have real leverage over how frontier AI is built and governed, before the terms are locked in by a handful of dominant actors.
sources.note: Aimed at officials and researchers, not the general public — the get-involved page explicitly invites policymakers, researchers and organisations. If you are none of those, the newsletter is realistically your only route. No verified donation route.

sources.jurisdiction: China (Beijing) and Singapore, with global engagement.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Build AI safety capacity and international coordination in and with China — better risk monitoring, standards input and cross-border dialogue.
sources.note: It is a social enterprise that consults for AI companies, so it is not a disinterested campaigner and takes no donations or volunteers. There is no advocacy route for a member of the public — its value to you is information.

sources.jurisdiction: United States — federal and, since 2026, state legislatures.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: The US government should take a proactive approach to AI governance that protects the public, including preserving states' ability to regulate AI rather than pre-empting them.
sources.note: No explicit volunteer or membership programme on its site — the realistic newcomer routes are the mailing list and money. Its leadership overlap with the Public First super PACs means supporting ARI is adjacent to electoral politics, which some people will not want.

sources.jurisdiction: United States, with a strong California state focus. Address: 584 Castro Street #3160, San Francisco.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Adopt policies that reduce the risk of severe harm from advanced AI, built on transparency, accountability and safe development.
sources.note: Its own website discloses no team, no board and no budget — you would be donating to an organisation whose scale is not public. Its ask is targeted transparency legislation, not a pause.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Align AI through better governance — workable international rules, EU implementation, and AI security policy, rather than leaving frontier development ungoverned.
sources.note: An insider policy shop. No campaign, no volunteering, no petitions — if you want to *do* something rather than fund or join it professionally, look elsewhere.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Change the incentives driving AI deployment, and establish new norms, legal protections and fundamental rights to preserve what makes human life meaningful in the age of AI.
sources.note: Framing is attention economy, mental health and social harm rather than extinction risk, though it covers both. High-profile media presence; less legislative throughput than Encode or Secure AI Project.

sources.jurisdiction: United States, with strong California state activity.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Children should be protected from unsafe AI — independent risk ratings for AI products, and states must keep the power to pass their own children's AI safety laws.
sources.note: Its frame is child safety and product harm, not catastrophic or existential risk. Broad public appeal but a narrower ask than the pause/ban groups — a good fit if your concern is kids and chatbots, a poor one if it is frontier capability.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: A new international treaty on autonomy in weapons systems, to ensure meaningful human control over the use of force.
sources.note: Covers autonomous weapons specifically, not general AI risk. If you belong to an organisation (a union branch, faith group, NGO), it will sign that organisation up as a member — the highest-leverage thing most people can do here.

sources.entity: Public First Action / Public First PAC
sources.jurisdiction: United States — federal and state races.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Elect and pressure federal and state politicians to back AI safeguards for children, workers and the public, stronger semiconductor export controls, and transparency from leading AI labs — and to resist federal pre-emption of state AI laws.
sources.note: This is partisan electoral money on both sides of the aisle, not charity — donations are not tax-deductible and will be spent attacking and supporting candidates. Reported to be backed by Anthropic employees and executives, which means an AI company's staff are funding one side of the AI safety fight; weigh that.

sources.entity: AI Money Watch (a project of Demand Progress)
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Make AI industry political spending visible, so voters can see who is paying for which candidate.
sources.note: Demand Progress's own homepage does not list AI as a focus area — AI Money Watch is a discrete project, so do not assume donating to Demand Progress funds AI work. The tracker's figures ($75.5M raised by Leading the Future, ~$70M cash on hand as of January 2026) come from FEC filings and will differ from press reports of total pledged commitments.

sources.jurisdiction: United States — federal and increasingly state races.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Elect politicians who will keep AI lightly regulated, and secure a single federal framework that pre-empts state AI laws.
sources.note: UNVERIFIED against the PAC's own site — figures here come from Wikipedia, Forbes, CNBC and the FEC-based AI Money Watch tracker, and 'raised', 'pledged' and 'cash on hand' are different numbers that press coverage often conflates. Reported controversies include an AI-generated news site using fake journalist personas (April 2026), $5,000-per-video payments to influencers pushing a China-threat message (May 2026), and an FEC complaint over shell-company payments (May 2026) — all allegations reported by third parties.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Shift public opinion toward AI deregulation and a federal framework pre-empting state laws.
sources.note: UNVERIFIED against its own site — figures from Forbes and Wikipedia. As a 501(c)(4) it does not disclose donors, so 'who is paying for this ad' is not answerable from public filings.

sources.jurisdiction: United States — state elections, with heavy California activity.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Stop states passing their own AI and tech rules; replace the 'patchwork' with a single permissive national approach.
sources.note: UNVERIFIED against Meta's own filings — figures from Axios, TechRepublic and GV Wire. This is separate from and additional to Leading the Future, so the two should not be added together casually, but they do point the same way.

sources.jurisdiction: United States — federal and all major state capitals.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Congress should pass a narrow, risk-based federal AI framework that pre-empts state AI laws, without private rights of action or mandatory independent audits.
sources.note: Stated fairly: TechNet is not anti-safety in its own framing — it supports the voluntary NIST AI Risk Management Framework and sector-specific laws. What it actively opposes is state-level binding rules, private lawsuits and mandatory audits. Its member list is at technet.org/our-story/members/.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: A national AI regulatory framework that is technology-neutral and risk-based and builds on existing law, rather than new rules that it says would hinder innovation and small businesses.
sources.note: CTA's own advocacy page does not explicitly state a position on federal pre-emption of state laws, though it has signed broader industry pre-emption coalition letters — treat any claim that CTA demands pre-emption as UNVERIFIED unless you find it in a specific filing.

sources.jurisdiction: United States — federal, state and courts.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Keep AI development and AI-generated work legally unencumbered — defend fair use for AI training, oppose broad restrictions on automated decision systems, and pursue a centre-left 'AI opportunity' agenda.
sources.note: Presents itself as progressive and center-left, which can make it read as civil society rather than industry — it is funded by tech companies and litigates on their side. If you are a writer, artist or musician, its copyright position is directly opposed to yours.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Clear the way for AI infrastructure — faster siting and permitting for data centres, fibre, subsea cables and power — under 'responsible and innovative AI policy'.
sources.note: Its AI interest is infrastructure and competition, not model capability — on frontier safety questions it is mostly absent. The concrete conflict is local: data centre siting, water and electricity.

sources.jurisdiction: United States primarily, with international policy work.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Regulate how AI is used — surveillance, algorithmic decisions, age-gating, encryption and competition — rather than restricting the technology itself; keep AI tools available and competitive.
sources.note: EFF is explicitly sceptical of broad AI regulation and of some safety-motivated proposals, and defends fair use for AI training. If your ask is 'slow AI down', EFF is not your ally on that point even though it is a genuine civil liberties organisation. It cannot take most cases referred to it.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: AI systems used on people — in policing, hiring, housing, healthcare, insurance and government — must be transparent, tested and accountable, and discriminatory screening and scoring tools should not be used.
sources.note: No public intake form for complaints — do not assume a tip will be acted on. Its focus is harm to identifiable people from deployed systems, not frontier or catastrophic risk.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Treat generative AI as a present danger: block federal deregulation and pre-emption of state AI laws, stop non-consensual AI images, and halt unchecked data centre build-out.
sources.note: Frames AI harm as consumer, labour and democratic harm happening now — it is generally dismissive of framing centred on future superintelligence. If you arrived via extinction-risk arguments, expect a different vocabulary.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: AI must be governed by binding, enforceable rules rooted in international human rights law — transparent, accountable and in the public interest — with particular scrutiny of biometric surveillance and AI in warfare.
sources.note: Its position is rights-based governance, not bans on AI development. The helpline is for people at risk, not a general complaints line — do not clog it with policy questions.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: AI products sold to consumers should be tested, transparent and accountable, and states should keep their role in regulating AI.
sources.note: Its AI landing page URL could not be confirmed — the domain and its AI positions are verified through CR's own press releases and research posts on advocacy.consumerreports.org, but treat any specific AI sub-page path as UNVERIFIED. Its focus is consumer protection, not catastrophic risk.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Consumers should be protected in digital markets and against fraud, including AI-enabled scams.
sources.note: FLAG: Which? has no dedicated AI policy programme that could be verified on its own site — AI appears inside fraud and digital markets work. If AI is your issue, this is a weaker route in the UK than approaching an MP directly or going through PauseAI UK or ControlAI.

sources.jurisdiction: European Union / Europe — 44 member organisations, 31 countries.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: The EU AI Act must give consumers real, enforceable rights — accountability, transparency and control over AI — and must not be hollowed out by the digital omnibus deregulation.
sources.note: BEUC does not take individual cases. Its influence is real but institutional; your leverage is through your national member organisation's campaigns.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Stop AI harms and bias — especially from facial recognition and biometric systems — by centring the people most affected and giving them a way to report what happened to them.
sources.note: Its remit is bias, biometrics and civil rights harm, not frontier model risk. Reporting a harm is not legal representation — AJL is not a law firm and cannot act on your case.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Challenge the current trajectory of AI by confronting industry concentration and power — antitrust scrutiny, limits on data centre expansion, and worker protection — rather than accepting scale as inevitable.
sources.note: A research institute, not a campaign — there is no petition, no membership and no volunteering. Its critique targets AI companies' power and is often explicitly at odds with the existential-risk framing used by groups like MIRI and ControlAI.

sources.jurisdiction: United States (IEEE-USA); IEEE standards work is global.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: US AI policy should be grounded in engineering reality: governance and regulation, safety, privacy and cybersecurity, IP protection, transparency, and a workforce pipeline matched to need.
sources.note: Route in is membership — non-members have essentially no path. Consensus position statements are slow and deliberately moderate; if you want an organisation to say something urgent, this is not the vehicle. The committee page does not spell out the joining process, so email first.

sources.entity: ACM Technology Policy Council (with USTPC and Europe TPC)
sources.jurisdiction: Global, with US and Europe committees.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Generative AI and algorithmic systems should be built and deployed according to published principles covering safety, intellectual property, workforce impact, accountability, transparency and fairness.
sources.note: The public policy pages do not explain how to volunteer for the committees — treat joining as UNVERIFIED and email the ACM Technology Policy Office. Principles are advisory and carry no enforcement.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Health AI must be ethical, equitable and responsible: disclosed to physicians and patients, overseen by clinicians, with clear rules on physician liability, data privacy, and limits on payers' use of automated decision-making.
sources.note: The AMA deliberately uses 'augmented intelligence' rather than 'artificial intelligence' to signal that AI should assist and not replace physicians — that framing is itself the position. Change happens through the House of Delegates resolution process, which is slow and requires membership and a sponsoring society.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: AI in the NHS must support and not supplant doctors, with clear principles for safe clinical use and protection of NHS patient data.
sources.note: UNVERIFIED: the principles PDF URL is on the BMA's own domain but was located via search rather than fetched, and the 2026 positions cited (NHS plan, NHS data warnings) come from third-party reporting. Confirm on bma.org.uk before relying on it. Route in is membership.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: AI in schools must be equitable, ethical and educator-led — with data privacy safeguards, rigorous vetting of tools for bias and effectiveness, and meaningful educator involvement in every adoption decision.
sources.note: Its ask is governance of classroom AI, not restrictions on AI development. Its guidance has drawn political attack over equity provisions, so expect the school board conversation to be contested. Members-only routes.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: AI's impact on the workplace should be a mandatory subject of collective bargaining, with contract language preventing worker displacement and a union seat at the table during development, procurement and implementation.
sources.note: AFT's stance is 'responsible and principled development and use' — it is not anti-AI and has partnered with AI companies on teacher training, which some members object to. The bargaining route is the genuinely powerful one; the policy statements are not binding on employers by themselves.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: Performers must control their own voice and likeness: informed consent and compensation for digital replicas in contracts, and a federal right for all Americans to control their likeness and voice via the NO FAKES Act.
sources.note: Its ask is control and consent over likeness, not limits on AI capability. The NO FAKES Act is contested by some digital rights groups (including EFF) as a broad new IP right that could restrict speech — you are picking a side in that argument by signing.

sources.jurisdiction: United States (film, TV and new media).
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: AI cannot write or rewrite literary material, cannot be credited, and cannot be used to undermine writers' credit or compensation — terms won in the 2023 Minimum Basic Agreement after a 148-day strike.
sources.note: Protections apply only to work covered by the MBA — non-union writing, and most AI training on already-published scripts, is not covered. Enforcement depends on writers actually reporting.

sources.jurisdiction: Global — affiliates in 148+ countries representing about 600,000 journalists.
sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: AI in the media must serve ethically-produced journalism, comply with the Global Charter of Ethics, and be governed by negotiated standards rather than imposed by employers.
sources.note: No individual membership — everything runs through your national union. Framework agreements are only as strong as each affiliate's ability to enforce them locally.

sources.label: Action page
sources.scope: AI must not be used to cut journalism jobs or degrade editorial standards; its use should be negotiated with the union, with transparency and protection of journalists' work.
sources.note: UNVERIFIED: the NUJ website blocked automated access, so the specific AI policy page URL and current wording could not be confirmed — only nuj.org.uk itself is given, and the 2026 industrial action is from third-party reporting (Personnel Today, Nieman Lab). Confirm directly. Route in is membership.
